top_findings.finding: One 60-day clock fits none of the four lines. Coffee buyers lapse at day 49, so the win-back flow reaches them 11 days late; brewing gear buyers lapse at day 364, so it reaches them 304 days early.
top_findings.evidence: Lapse points are the 80th percentile of 214 coffee and 39 brewing gear repeat gaps; the flow's delay is 60 days for everyone.
top_findings.action: Split the existing flow by the line of the last order and set each branch's delay to that line's lapse point, instead of adding a second win-back flow.

top_findings.finding: 23 of the flow's 37 recipients in the last 90 days were not lapsed yet by their own pace, and 2 of them used the 15% code on an order placed before their own lapse point.
top_findings.evidence: Flow recipients rebuilt from the order history; the code cost about $20.64 on those orders.
top_findings.action: Move the code out of the second email; offer the margin-capped amount only to lapsed customers from the second touch.

top_findings.finding: 48 customers are past their lapse point and still inside the stop point. The 18 repeat buyers among them spent about $6,823 a year at their old pace; the other 30 bought once, so they have no pace to price.
top_findings.evidence: All 48 have $6,732 in lifetime revenue and $3,358 in lifetime gross margin; the yearly figure is the plan rows' yearly value at the old pace, repeat buyers only.
top_findings.action: Run the lapsed plan below, repeat buyers first; they have bought the line more than once.

top_findings.finding: Brewing gear buyers who come back buy coffee beans, not more gear: 29 of the 34 returning first-time gear buyers (85%).
top_findings.evidence: Second orders of customers whose first order was brewing gear, from the order table.
top_findings.action: Lead the gear win-back with beans for the machine they own; another machine is the wrong reason to return.
